notes: Edition composed by Claude from the collected headlines, reading titles and metadata only.
Each narrative is an idea that joins several different events; what it joins is listed at the top. It commits to a claim, and the last rung of every narrative is the case against it. Read both.
Where a narrative continues one from the previous edition it says what has changed since; every edition is kept, so the reader can step back to where we were.

Each narrative ends with 'How we got here': four horizons, since 2020, since 2008, since 1989 and since 1945, each the start of a regime the headlines are living inside, and sometimes a fifth that reaches further back and names its own starting year. They are a trajectory, not a verdict.

Each narrative sets one or two things to watch for: what should follow, by when, if its join is right. Later editions check them against their headlines; the ledger is data/watch.json and the count stands beside the narrative's firmness.
The connections are made by the model, not by the publishers. Follow any headline to the original report before repeating it.
Books and trajectories appear only where they change how a fragment or a horizon reads.

readings.line: Taiwan's fastest growth in fifty years rests on AI spending, so when US tech shares fall its state funds and central bank step in.

watch.what: Taiwan's National Stabilization Fund or central bank reports further buying of shares or Taiwan dollars during November.
watch.because: If Taiwan's market is now tied to doubts about US AI spending, further falls in US tech should bring further Taiwanese state action, not a single week's support.

watch.what: South Korea's government or a state fund announces support for chip shares or the won as tech stocks fall.
watch.because: The join says chip-supplying economies now carry AI risk on public books, and South Korea is the other large supplier exposed to the same spending.

readings.change: The markdown of the AI spenders deepened: Alphabet had its biggest fall on record, Intel lost 29% and the Nasdaq is on course for a $2 trillion October loss. What is new is where it lands. Taiwan reported record foreign selling of its shares and record buying by its state funds, while its central bank defended the currency.
readings.claim: A US tech sell-off over AI spending, with the Nasdaq facing a $2 trillion October loss and Intel down 29% in a day, came in the same week that Taiwan reported its fastest growth in half a century, foreign investors sold nearly a trillion Taiwan dollars of its shares in a month, and Taiwan's state funds and central bank bought to steady the market and the currency. The AI investment wave has tied Taiwan's output to the spending plans of a handful of American companies. When investors in New York doubt those plans, the losses they want to avoid are partly taken on by Taiwanese public money.

events.label: US tech shares fall over AI spending
Big Tech spends cash instead of paying out
Taiwan's record growth and record foreign selling
Taiwan's state fund and central bank intervene
Chip makers elsewhere sold and expanded

rungs.label: The US sell-off and its cause

fragments.label: Falls in New York and elsewhere
fragments.text: The Star in Malaysia reports the Nasdaq facing a $2 trillion October wipeout as fears about AI spending deepen. Handelsblatt reports Intel shares down 29 percent as the Nasdaq 100 slid, and BBC News Brasil asks whether the AI bubble has burst after Alphabet's biggest drop in its history. Walla in Israel and Länsi-Savo in Finland report the same fall in their own markets, with AI giants losing ground.

fragments.label: Spending ahead of shareholders
fragments.text: The Star reports that Big Tech is returning the smallest share of its cash to shareholders in 15 years because of AI spending. Fortune writes that Amazon's spending is overshadowing its growth, and a Berkeley law professor in Fortune treats Anthropic's planned listing as a test of AI accountability. The money is going into data centres and chips rather than back to investors.

fragments.label: Record growth, record selling
fragments.text: UDN reports Taiwan's growth over the first three quarters at 14.22%, the highest in half a century. The same paper reports foreign investors sold nearly a trillion Taiwan dollars of local shares this month, the worst on record, while state funds bought a record 240.9 billion. ETtoday reports the market almost 10% below its highs and waiting on chip results.

fragments.label: The state steps in
fragments.text: UDN quotes the National Stabilization Fund saying it is normal for stocks to rise and fall, and reports the central bank intervening forcefully to hold the Taiwan dollar at 32.520. Yicai reports net selling of SMIC by southbound Hong Kong funds of HK$999 million. In Germany, NDR reports Vishay expanding its chip plant in Itzehoe, so building continues while the shares fall.

fragments.label: From shareholders to the state
fragments.text: The American companies have chosen to spend their cash on AI rather than return it, which leaves the bet with their investors. Taiwan sells the chips that spending buys, so its record growth is the same bet seen from the supplier's side. When foreign funds sell Taiwanese shares to cut their exposure, Taiwan's state funds and central bank take some of it on. Part of the AI boom is now carried on a public balance sheet in Taipei.

fragments.label: A routine intervention
fragments.text: Taiwan's stabilisation fund has bought in most large sell-offs since it was set up, so a record purchase may show the size of this fall rather than a new role for the state. Foreign selling in Taipei can also follow the currency, US pressure on Chinese firms, which China's foreign ministry protested this week in Yicai, or security worries such as ETtoday's report of a Chinese spy near Jensen Huang. The events also part: Intel is losing the AI chip race, Alphabet is a spender, and Taiwan is a supplier booking real profits rather than losses.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The years since 2020 turned the chip from a component into an object of state policy. In 2021 a shortage of microcontrollers stopped car plants in Germany, the United States and Japan, and governments learned how much of the supply came from a few fabs in Taiwan. Washington answered with the CHIPS and Science Act of August 2022, worth about $52 billion in subsidies, and TSMC agreed to build in Arizona. Three months later ChatGPT reached a hundred million users, and demand for the graphics chips that train such models went from a niche to the largest order book in the industry. By these headlines the result is visible in UDN's figure of 14.22% growth for Taiwan in the first three quarters, a half-century high. The same years made a few American spenders the main customers, so Taiwan's growth and the Nasdaq's fears now depend on the same orders.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: After Lehman Brothers failed in September 2008, central banks held interest rates near zero for most of a decade and bought bonds by the trillion. Cheap money and the smartphone made the platform companies the largest firms on earth, and from about 2012 they returned much of their cash through buybacks and dividends; Apple alone has bought back several hundred billion dollars of its own shares since then. Adam Tooze's Crashed describes how that decade's rescues kept capital flowing to the safest-looking assets, and the cloud companies were among them. The Star's report that Big Tech is now returning the smallest share of its cash in 15 years marks the end of that habit: the money is going into data centres instead. Taiwan's National Stabilization Fund, which bought shares in the 2008 crash and in later sell-offs, was used throughout that era against sudden foreign outflows, and is being used again now.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The industry Taiwan now depends on was built in the years around the end of the Cold War. TSMC was founded in 1987 by Morris Chang with state backing, on the idea that one company could make chips for many designers who owned no factories. Through the 1990s the fabless model spread, the WTO opened markets, and Taiwan became the factory for American chip design. The same decade taught markets how to price a technology before it earned anything: Netscape's listing in 1995, then the Nasdaq's fall of almost four fifths between March 2000 and October 2002. Taiwan passed the law creating its National Stabilization Fund in 2000, during that crash. The Fortune piece on Anthropic's listing and BBC Brasil's question about a bubble both measure the present against that precedent, though today's spenders have earnings that the dot-com firms lacked.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The habit of the state buying shares in Taipei belongs to a longer pattern. After 1949 the Kuomintang government on Taiwan, backed by American aid until 1965, ran a state-led industrial policy: land reform, an export processing zone at Kaohsiung from 1966, the Industrial Technology Research Institute in 1973 and the Hsinchu Science Park in 1980. In the United States the same postwar decades had governments paying for the technologies that mattered, from the 1956 Dartmouth workshop that named artificial intelligence to ARPA after Sputnik. What has changed is who pays first. The AI build-out is financed by private companies, as the Star's report on shrinking payouts shows, while the state reappears afterwards as buyer of last resort, in UDN's report of record purchases by Taiwan's state funds. The postwar developmental state is still there, but as a stabiliser rather than a sponsor.

readings.line: With oil near $118, the war's price rise is now argued over in wage talks, while governments cut fuel and sales taxes to slow it.

watch.what: A national strike or wage settlement in a European country is reported with fuel or energy prices named among its reasons.
watch.because: If the war's price rise has moved from the pump into pay, the next large pay disputes should cite it, which neither the oil price nor any single wage round predicts alone.

watch.what: Japan's Diet passes the consumption tax reduction bill.
watch.because: If governments are still choosing to absorb the price rise through tax rather than leave it to wages, Japan's bill should pass rather than stall.

readings.change: The previous edition followed Washington's push for a lower oil price and the fuel taxes being reset elsewhere. Brent has since risen another 2.4%. Fuel relief continues in Turkey and Germany, but the price rise now also shows in inflation figures and pay claims, in Italy, Colombia, Nigeria and Vietnam.
readings.claim: Brent crude reached $117.64 as India's foreign minister warned the G20 of energy disruptions, Italy's inflation rose to 5.4% with its president blaming stagnant wages, Italian protesters demanded the government lay down arms and raise pay, and Colombia, Nigeria and Vietnam opened minimum wage or public pay rounds. In the same days Turkey paid back fuel tax, Germany argued over whether its fuel discount reaches drivers and Japan's parliament debated a consumption tax cut. The question of who pays for the price rise from the war with Iran is moving from governments' tax receipts to employers' payrolls. That makes it a question about next year's wages, not only this month's pump prices.

events.label: Brent rises as the Gulf war continues
Italian inflation and protests over pay
Minimum and public pay rounds open
Fuel and consumption tax relief
Halloween sweets cost more

rungs.label: The oil price and the relief

fragments.label: The price
fragments.text: Jornal Económico reports Brent for December delivery up 2.40% to $117.64 a barrel. BusinessLine reports Jaishankar warning the G20 of global energy supply disruptions, while Anadolu carries Trump saying the war with Iran will end soon. Philstar expects petrol prices higher next week in the Philippines, and NDR reports German heating oil suppliers overwhelmed by orders at high prices.

fragments.label: The relief
fragments.text: Hürriyet's Bigpara reports fuel tax refunds of 29.3 billion lira being paid into accounts in Turkey. Handelsblatt asks how much of Germany's fuel discount actually reaches drivers. Asahi reports Japan's consumption tax reduction bill at its climax with the benefits still unclear. Each government is paying out of its tax take to hold prices down at the point of sale.

fragments.label: Italy
fragments.text: Il Messaggero reports Italian inflation rising to 5.4%, with President Mattarella saying the standard of living is under attack from stagnant wages and rising prices. Minuto Uno in Argentina reports mass protests against Giorgia Meloni under the slogan 'Lay down arms and raise wages'.

fragments.label: Minimum wage rounds and shop prices
fragments.text: El Universal reports that Fenalco, Colombia's retail federation, will return to the 2027 minimum wage talks and has already put forward an increase. Daily Post Nigeria carries a cleric's argument that the government cannot pay workers the 500,000 naira labour wants. In Vietnam, An ninh Thủ đô reports the home affairs minister proposing new pay and allowances for commune-level public employees. In Britain and the US, BBC News and Ideastream report shoppers alarmed by the cost of Halloween sweets.

rungs.label: Who pays for the price rise

fragments.label: From the budget to the payroll
fragments.text: In the first months of a price shock, governments pay through tax cuts and refunds, as Turkey, Germany and Japan are doing. Once the rise shows in the annual inflation figure, it enters the wage claims that employers and treasuries settle for a year or more, as in Italy, Colombia and Nigeria. The Italian slogan joins the two halves: it treats arms spending and the fall in real pay as one budget choice. In each place the cost of the war is being moved from the fuel price to the question of what a year's work is worth.

fragments.label: Old fights with their own causes
fragments.text: Nigeria's minimum wage dispute grows out of its own currency fall and the end of its petrol subsidy, and Colombia sets its minimum wage every December whatever oil does. Vietnam's public pay reform has been planned for years, and Japan's consumption tax cut is an election-season measure. Halloween sweets owe more to cocoa than to crude. What these events do not share is a single cause: only Italy's inflation figure and the fuel relief schemes clearly carry the oil price, and the rest may be ordinary annual pay politics in a year when oil happens to be high.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The years since 2020 taught governments a routine for oil shocks. After Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Brent passed $130 in March, euro area inflation peaked at 10.6% that October, and the ECB raised rates from July 2022. Governments paid first at the pump: Germany's three-month fuel discount in the summer of 2022, Italy's cut in fuel excise, France's rebate at the till. Economists then argued, as Handelsblatt argues now, over how much of each discount reached drivers and how much stayed with the oil companies. Wages followed late and only in part, and Italian real pay fell further in 2022 than in most large economies. By these headlines a second shock has come from the Gulf, after the twelve-day war of June 2025 was followed by a longer one, and the same sequence is running again, with Mattarella's remark about stagnant wages arriving where the 2022 sequence ended.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: Brent reached $147 in July 2008 and fell below $40 by December as the financial crisis cut demand. For the next decade wages in southern Europe barely moved: austerity after the euro crisis of 2010 to 2012 kept Italian pay flat, and the habit of low settlements outlasted the crisis. Over the same years the oil price came to depend on Gulf security more than on supply. The Iran nuclear agreement of July 2015 lowered the risk premium on crude; the United States' withdrawal in 2018 restored it, and the drone and missile strike on Abqaiq in September 2019 showed that cheap weapons could halve Saudi output for days. Jaishankar's warning to the G20 about supply disruption comes from a large importer that has lived with this risk since. Italy's protesters now connect that Gulf risk to pay that has hardly risen in fifteen years.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: In the 1990s the link between prices and wages was cut by law and by the world market. Italy abolished the scala mobile, its automatic wage indexation, in the July 1992 agreement between government, unions and employers, so that pay since has followed bargaining rather than the price index. Colombia's 1991 constitution and a 1996 law gave a commission of government, employers and unions the job of setting the minimum wage each December, with the government deciding by decree if talks fail; that is the table Fenalco is returning to. Vietnam's reforms after 1986 and the entry of China and India into world trade added hundreds of millions of workers to global labour supply and held down the price of manufactured goods for two decades. Karl Polanyi's argument in The Great Transformation, that societies eventually try to pull labour back out of the market, describes what the Italian protest and the Nigerian claim are attempting.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The postwar order priced the world economy in dollars and its energy in Gulf oil. In February 1945 Roosevelt and Ibn Saud made an unwritten bargain of protection for oil, and for almost thirty years cheap crude underwrote rising pay in Europe and Japan. The Arab embargo of October 1973 quadrupled the price, and the decade that followed was defined by wage-price spirals: indexed pay in Italy, strikes in Britain, and governments trying incomes policies to stop prices and wages chasing each other. Daniel Yergin's The Prize tells how that fuel became the organising fact of the century's wars and alliances. The lesson governments drew from the 1970s was to keep oil prices out of wage settlements, and the present headlines, from Turkey's fuel tax refund to Italy's 5.4% inflation, show them trying to hold that line once more.

readings.line: More than four years into the invasion, European ministers shun Russia while Washington and African governments negotiate with it.

watch.what: The US Treasury lifts or eases sanctions on a named Russian official, company or fund.
watch.because: If Washington is treating Russia as a negotiating partner while Europe isolates it, the reported overture on sanctions should become an act that Europe does not copy.

watch.what: A European government or the EU publicly objects to a US step to ease Russia sanctions or to the terms of the Abu Dhabi talks.
watch.because: The join predicts that the gap between European isolation and American bargaining becomes an open dispute between allies, not only a difference of tone.

readings.claim: European ministers refused to stand beside Sergei Lavrov for the G20 family photograph, Poland's foreign minister told him 'enough', and Moscow called the German foreign minister's conduct 'the bottom', in the same days that US and Russian foreign ministers discussed coordination at APEC, Washington weighed lifting sanctions on a Putin associate, Russia signed 53 documents at its Africa summit and Nigeria moved to replace a 59-year-old air agreement with Moscow. Europe treats Russia as an outcast, while the United States and several African governments treat it as a partner to bargain and trade with. The division over Russia now runs between Washington and its European allies as well as between Europe and Africa, even as Washington approves 500 Patriot missiles for Ukraine.

events.label: Europeans shun Lavrov at the G20
US talks with Moscow and weighs sanctions
Russia's agreements with African states
US approves Patriot sale to Ukraine
Oleshky truce while Kremlin keeps fighting

fragments.label: The G20 photograph
fragments.text: Länsi-Savo in Finland reports that the G20 group photo was cancelled because European countries refused to stand alongside Lavrov, and Habertürk in Turkey notes the meeting began before any family photo was taken. Onet reports Radosław Sikorski telling Lavrov 'Enough of this', and Radio Zet says he addressed a message to Russians through a man close to Putin. Izvestia and Lenta quote Maria Zakharova calling Johann Wadephul's behaviour toward Lavrov 'the bottom' and an attempt to scare him with 'naked diplomacy'.

fragments.label: Washington
fragments.text: 47NEWS reports the US and Russian foreign ministers discussing coordination at APEC, with China arranging a three-way leaders' meeting. La Dépêche reports Washington considering lifting sanctions on the man it calls Putin's 'black box'. Kommersant quotes Yuri Ushakov saying Russia and the US are agreeing a date for Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, and UNIAN reports Kyiv's foreign ministry describing Europe's role there. Kommersant also reports Melania Trump announcing the evacuation of more than 750 residents from Oleshky, and NZ Herald reports locals using a rare truce to leave.

fragments.label: Africa
fragments.text: Youm7 in Egypt reports the Kremlin saying 53 government and joint documents were signed on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa summit. Leadership reports Nigeria and Russia moving to replace their 59-year-old air services agreement, and Lenta reports the US assessing Russian sales of Su-35S fighters and S-400 air defences to Ethiopia.

fragments.label: Refusal, bargaining and trade
fragments.text: Europe's instruments are refusal and sanctions: its ministers will not be photographed with Russia's foreign minister. Washington's are bargaining: it talks to Moscow and considers easing sanctions, and in the same days Daily Post, ENIKOS, UNIAN and ANSA report it approving 500 Patriot missiles for Ukraine for $2.1 billion. African governments deal with Russia as a supplier of aircraft, weapons and air links. The Kremlin, in UNIAN's report, says it will keep fighting during negotiations, so it can work each of these channels separately.

fragments.label: Less of a split than it looks
fragments.text: Refusing a photograph is a gesture at a meeting the Europeans still attended, and UNIAN reports Europe has a role in the Abu Dhabi talks, so Europe is not outside the bargaining. The Patriot sale shows Washington still arming Ukraine, and the sanctions idea is only under consideration. Nigeria's air agreement dates from 1967 and Ethiopia's Russian arms go back to the Soviet period, so the African deals are old ties renewed, not a response to Washington's turn. What the events do not share is an aim: the US contacts are about ending a war, the African ones are trade and arms, and the European ones are about who is seen with whom.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The present arrangement was set in 2022. After the invasion of 24 February, the EU adopted package after package of sanctions, froze Russian central bank reserves with the G7 and closed its airspace to Russian aircraft. In the UN General Assembly vote of 2 March 2022, 141 states condemned the invasion, but 35 abstained, many of them African, and most governments outside Europe and North America declined to join the sanctions. Russia held its second Africa summit in St Petersburg in July 2023. G20 meetings since have struggled over Russia's presence, and walkouts and refused photographs became the European way of registering it. The change by these headlines is in Washington: the Trump administration's direct talks with Moscow, from 2025, ended the common Western line. The cancelled family photo reported by Länsi-Savo and the APEC coordination reported by 47NEWS show the two halves of that change in one week.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: The August 2008 war in Georgia was followed within a year by an American reset with Moscow. The habit of treating Russia as an outcast began instead in 2014: when Russia annexed Crimea that March, the other members suspended the G8, and the EU and US imposed the first sectoral sanctions. From then Moscow looked elsewhere: to China, with a gas deal in May 2014, and to Africa, where Wagner contractors arrived in the Central African Republic in 2018 and the first Russia-Africa summit was held in Sochi in October 2019. The 53 documents signed at this week's summit, in Youm7's report, continue that line. Washington's policy swung in these years between the reset of 2009, sanctions in 2014 and the Helsinki summit of 2018, so its present overture has precedent, while Europe's position has moved in one direction since 2014.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: After 1991 Russia was invited in. It joined the Council of Europe in 1996, and the G7 became the G8 when Russia was admitted in 1997. NATO and the EU then expanded east, taking in Poland in 1999 and 2004. Ivan Krastev and Stephen Holmes argue in The Light That Failed that the decades after 1989 were an age of imitating the West, and that Russia's reply was to imitate what it saw as Western hypocrisy rather than Western institutions. The colour revolutions, from Tbilisi in 2003 to Kyiv in 2004, convinced Moscow that every crowd was a Western project. Sikorski, a minister in Polish governments since the 2000s, is a figure of that enlargement, and his 'enough' to Lavrov in Onet's report comes from the country that most wanted to leave Moscow's sphere and now most wants Russia kept out.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The African ties are older than the end of the Cold War. From the late 1950s the Soviet Union offered newly independent states arms, scholarships and aid without the colonial record of London and Paris; in 1956 it backed Nasser over Suez and learned that an outside power could make itself the guarantor of a settlement. During Nigeria's civil war, which began in 1967, Moscow supplied the federal government with aircraft when Britain hesitated, and the air services agreement Leadership reports Nigeria replacing dates from that year. In 1977 the Soviet Union switched sides in the Horn of Africa and armed Ethiopia, which is why Lenta can report Su-35S and S-400 sales to Addis Ababa as a continuation. Tony Judt's Postwar describes the opposite memory in Europe, where Soviet power meant occupation, and the two memories now support opposite policies toward the same state.

readings.line: Protests called for the same weekend in several European countries are met with bans in some cities and negotiation in others.

watch.what: Organisers in two or more European countries announce a shared date for a further protest in November.
watch.because: If these are one wave rather than local grievances that happened to meet on a weekend, the next call should again be made across borders.

watch.what: A European government proposes new limits on face coverings or on public gatherings, citing the 31 October protests.
watch.because: The join is about how states set the limits of assembly, and a wave across countries should produce a rule rather than only one day's policing decision.

readings.claim: Shopkeepers in The Hague are taking precautions against a possible 'Gen Z protest', La Rochelle has banned gatherings on 31 October while Rochefort and Saintes allow them within set perimeters, Lisbon's police say they have no red lines for the demonstration on the 31st at Rossio, more than 150,000 young Germans have signed up for street protests, Italians marched against Giorgia Meloni, and arrests were threatened at a large protest outside the US embassy in London. The grievances are separate, from housing in Lisbon to wages and arms in Italy, but they reach the street in the same days. Each state is deciding the same question, how much public space a crowd may take, on its own terms, from a prefect's ban to a police negotiator.

events.label: Hague shops brace for Gen Z protest
German youth sign up for protests
French towns ban or allow gatherings
Lisbon housing camps and Rossio demonstration
Italian protests over arms and wages
London protest at the US embassy

fragments.label: Netherlands and Germany
fragments.text: NOS reports shopkeepers in The Hague taking precautions against a possible 'Gen Z protest'. Yle in Finland reports German young people taking to the streets, with more than 150,000 signed up for protests. Neither headline names the grievance.

fragments.label: France and Portugal
fragments.text: Sud Ouest lists where people may protest in Charente-Maritime on Saturday 31 October: gatherings remain banned in La Rochelle and are allowed in Rochefort and Saintes within set perimeters. Franceinfo asks whether Halloween masks can be banned the next day. In Lisbon, Observador reports the PSP police saying they have no red lines for the demonstration on the 31st but rule out 'endless dialogue' at Rossio. The same paper reports emigrants' open letter backing the housing encampments, and Pureza attacking the consensus on golden visas and tax breaks.

fragments.label: Italy and Britain
fragments.text: Minuto Uno in Argentina reports mass protests in Italy against Meloni under the slogan 'Lay down arms and raise wages'. Walla in Israel reports tension in London, with arrests threatened at a large protest outside the US embassy.

fragments.label: Many grievances, one weekend
fragments.text: The grievances differ: housing and golden visas in Lisbon, pay and arms spending in Italy, US policy in London, and in The Hague and Germany a generation named rather than a cause. What they share is timing and form, crowds of mostly young people in central squares in the same days, which is how protest has spread since the Gen Z movements in Asia and Africa. The response is national and often municipal: a prefectoral ban in La Rochelle, permitted perimeters in nearby towns, a police negotiator in Lisbon and private precautions by Dutch shops. Franceinfo's question about Halloween masks shows a festival object becoming a policing question because the festival and the protests fall on the same day.

fragments.label: A weekend, not a wave
fragments.text: 31 October is a Saturday before a public holiday in France and Portugal, so protests of every kind fall on it, and no headline names a common organiser or slogan. Lisbon's demonstration grows out of a housing camp with its own history, London's is about US policy, and the German sign-ups may concern a different date and a domestic issue such as military service, which Yle's headline does not state. The La Rochelle ban may have purely local reasons. What the events do not share is a demand, and the pattern may be an artefact of a collection gathered on the eve of one weekend.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The years since 2020 changed both sides of the protest. Lockdowns in 2020 and 2021 gave European states emergency powers over gatherings, and France and Portugal used them repeatedly; the habit of perimeter orders and prefectoral bans outlived the virus. On the other side, a generation organised on TikTok, Discord and Telegram produced protests that named themselves by age: Sri Lanka in 2022, Kenya's finance bill protests in June 2024, Bangladesh's students in July and August 2024, and Nepal in September 2025, where a government fell to protesters carrying a pirate flag from a Japanese comic. Morocco and Madagascar followed within weeks. By these headlines the label has now reached The Hague, where NOS reports shopkeepers preparing for a 'Gen Z protest', and the question for European police is whether a movement without leaders can be negotiated with, as Lisbon's PSP proposes, or only banned.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: The housing grievance in Lisbon was assembled after 2008. Portugal took a €78 billion rescue in 2011, cut public pay and pensions, and courted foreign money to recover: a tax regime for non-habitual residents from 2009, and golden visas for property buyers from 2012. Tourism and short-term letting followed, and Lisbon rents rose faster than wages through the 2010s. The protests of that decade set the form: Cairo's Tahrir Square in early 2011, Portugal's 'Geração à Rasca' march that March, and Madrid's Puerta del Sol camp that May, where occupying a central square became the method. Pureza's attack in Observador on the consensus over golden visas, and the emigrants' letter backing the encampments, belong to this line, the letter written partly by Portuguese who left during the crisis. The Rossio demonstration applies the camp method to rent.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The European protest against a foreign war, like Italy's 'lay down arms' and London's march to the US embassy, took its present form after the Cold War. The counter-summit protests of Seattle in 1999 and Genoa in 2001, where a protester was shot dead during the G8, made Italian police and the Italian left long adversaries. On 15 February 2003 millions marched in London, Rome and Madrid against the invasion of Iraq; the war went ahead, and many concluded that numbers alone change nothing. Belgrade in October 2000 had offered the opposite lesson, that a disciplined movement could bring down a government. Europe's protesters still choose between the two models. The slogan reported by Minuto Uno joins arms and wages in one demand, as the 2003 marches did not, which reflects years in which defence spending and pay compete in the same budget.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The right being negotiated in each city was written into the postwar constitutions. Italy's of 1948 guarantees peaceful assembly in Article 17, requiring only notice for public places; West Germany's Basic Law of 1949 does so in Article 8; Portugal's of 1976, written after the Carnation Revolution of April 1974, made demonstration a right for a people denied it for forty-eight years. France kept an older regime, a 1935 decree requiring demonstrations to be declared, which is why a prefect in Charente-Maritime can ban gatherings in one town and allow them in another, as Sud Ouest reports. May 1968 in Paris fixed the script of young people in the street and the state's replies to them. Elias Canetti's Crowds and Power asks what a crowd wants once it has formed; these laws are the postwar answer to how much space it may take.
